# The Agent Operating Surface

The glassfrog CLI is built for AI agents as much as for people. But an agent
driving a command-line tool starts each session blind — it has to rediscover how
to get parseable output, how to page, what an exit code means, how credentials
are supplied — and it can mis-drive the tool, including running a governance write
nobody approved. The **Agent Operating Surface** is a thin, agent-facing layer
that rides on top of the CLI to close that gap. This document explains what it is,
why it is shaped as it is, and where it deliberately stops.

The surface has two parts so far: **Operator Orientation** (packaged operating
knowledge) and the **Write-Safety Guardrail** (enforced confirmation of governance
writes). Both are delivered as one Claude plugin. Critically, the layer adds **no
API capability of its own** — every fact it packages and every command it gates is
about behaviour the CLI already exposes. It is knowledge and enforcement, never a
new surface.

## Why a plugin of skills, and why one skill first

The orientation knowledge ships as a Claude plugin homed in a dedicated top-level
`plugin/` directory (a manifest plus `plugin/skills/`), kept separate from the Go
CLI code. The alternative — making the whole repo the plugin root — was rejected
because it conflates a Go CLI repo with a plugin and leaves later additions (a
marketplace, more skills) nowhere natural to sit.

Within the plugin, the knowledge is one **orientation skill** today, not several
fine-grained ones. A single skill keeps tightly-related knowledge together and
matches how it is consumed — triggered on demand by description, not loaded up
front. The `plugin/skills/` directory is the extension point: the guardrail and,
later, the operator paths (navigation, tension processing, proposal flows) arrive
as *sibling* skills, so the surface grows additively rather than being
restructured. If the single skill ever grows unwieldy, splitting it later is cheap
precisely because consumers trigger by description, not by a fixed file set.

## Why the orientation is hand-authored, and points at the CLI for command detail

The orientation content is hand-authored, committed prose — not generated from the
CLI. That is a deliberate departure from the npm packaging channel, which
*generates* its output from source because it is pure mechanical repackaging.
Orientation is mostly judgement — parsing strategy, how to *react* to each exit
code, write-safety expectations — and judgement has no machine source to generate
from. So it is written prose a reviewer can read.

The one thing it refuses to duplicate is the per-command, per-flag catalogue. That
detail is the largest drift surface — it goes stale the moment a command or flag
changes — so orientation points at the CLI's own `glassfrog <command> --help`
instead, keeping command detail single-sourced in the CLI. What remains in the
skill is a small, stable set of cross-cutting facts (the four output-format names,
the `0`–`8` exit-code meanings, the credential command, pagination). Because that
residual surface is small and enumerable, a best-effort drift guard in
`internal/build` can pin it: it asserts the format tokens, exit codes, and the
`auth login` command the skill names still match their CLI source, and fails the
build when a documented anchor drifts. The guard is explicitly *partial* — it
pins what is mechanically checkable and leaves the judgement prose to review — and
that partiality is stated rather than hidden.

## Why write-safety is enforced by a hook, not a skill or a CLI flag

Orientation *describes* write-safety — confirm before writing; on a `412` stale
write, re-read and re-confirm rather than blindly retrying — but it cannot
*enforce* it. A skill is guidance the agent may ignore. Enforcement is a separate
capability, and its central design question was **where** to enforce.

Three options were weighed:

- **A skill** (instructional). This matches orientation's pattern but fails the
  requirement outright: a skill cannot stop an agent from self-authorizing a
  write.
- **A CLI-level gate** (an interactive prompt or a `--force`/`--yes` flag on the
  write commands). This was already rejected once, when withdraw-proposal was
  designed: it breaks the CLI's non-interactive, agent-driven contract (an agent
  can't answer a prompt) and would be the first write to gate itself, forking the
  uniform write surface. That earlier decision explicitly deferred destructive-write
  confirmation to *this* guardrail, to gate writes across the whole path centrally.
- **An operator-layer `PreToolUse` hook.** The plugin host intercepts the agent's
  `Bash` call *before* it runs and can route it to a human decision.

The hook won because it is the only option that genuinely *enforces*: the agent
physically cannot run the command until the host's decision resolves. It gates
centrally across the proposal write path rather than per-command, and it lives off
the CLI entirely, so the CLI's write surface stays uniform and untouched. An agent
driving the bare CLI with no plugin still acts without a prompt — the human
checkpoint is added at the operator layer, not baked into the command-is-intent
contract the CLI keeps.

## Why the gate returns "ask" instead of "deny"

The confirmation model is a mandatory human-in-the-loop checkpoint: the agent
cannot self-authorize a governance write. A `PreToolUse` hook can return `allow`,
`deny`, or `ask`. The guardrail returns **"ask"** — the host surfaces the exact
command, its target, and its effect to the human and runs it only on explicit
approval.

The alternative, `deny` plus a conversational instruction to "go ask the
practitioner in chat," was rejected because it relies on the agent faithfully
relaying and interpreting a free-text exchange — softer, and it re-introduces
agent judgement into the gate. With `ask`, the decision is the human's, made
against the literal command; the agent neither answers it nor can bypass it, and
no bespoke confirmation UI has to be built. The reason string names *what changes*
— the command, target, and effect — and nothing about whether the change is
governance-sound (that would be coaching, which the surface excludes).

## Why governance writes are recognized by a static, fail-closed registry

The CLI gives the hook no signal about whether a command writes — adding one would
be new CLI capability, which the surface forbids. So the hook must classify from
the `Bash` command string alone. Rather than a brittle heuristic (any command
containing `propose`/`withdraw`), it uses a **static registry** of the four
proposal-write leaves (`proposal create`, `proposal propose`, `proposal respond`,
`proposal withdraw`). It resolves the actual `glassfrog` invocation and its
subcommand path — handling an absolute path, an env-var prefix, and arguments —
then gates only when the path is a registered write leaf. Reads and operational
tension edits pass.

Within the `proposal` namespace the registry is **fail-closed**: an *unrecognized*
`proposal` subcommand is gated rather than waved through, so a future write leaf is
safe-by-default until the registry is updated. That registry is the single place
that encodes "what is a governance write," consumed by both the hook and a
best-effort `internal/build` drift tripwire. If the CLI gains or renames a
proposal write command without the registry being updated, the tripwire turns the
build red — closing the hole where a new write could silently ship ungated.

## Why the guardrail doesn't re-author the stale-write protocol

Orientation already states the `412` re-read-and-re-confirm expectation as
guidance, and content must not be duplicated across the surface. So the guardrail
adds *enforcement*, not new guidance. It doesn't re-author the re-read protocol;
instead, because the hook gates *every* proposal-path write, a retry after a `412`
is itself gated and requires fresh human confirmation. "No blind retry" therefore
holds structurally — the retry can't run un-confirmed — while the re-read step
stays single-sourced in orientation. The hook does not itself perform or verify
the re-read (it can't inject state); it only guarantees the retry can't run
without a new confirmation.

## Design boundaries and an accepted limit

The surface deliberately stops short of several things:

- **It adds no CLI capability.** No command, flag, output format, or behaviour
  beyond what the CLI (and thus the v5 API) already provides. It is knowledge and
  enforcement riding on the CLI, never a second surface that could drift.
- **It re-validates nothing.** The API is the source of truth; confirmation is
  about operator *intent*, not re-deciding whether a change is correct. Local
  governance logic would inevitably drift from the spec.
- **It does not coach Holacracy.** The surface orients on driving the CLI safely;
  assessing whether a governance change is *wise* is facilitation, a different
  concern it explicitly excludes.
- **It does not gate reads or operational tension edits.** A tension is an
  operational item, not a governance change; only the proposal write path carries
  the confirmation cost, so the agent's primary mode — legible reads — stays fast.
- **It does not define its own distribution.** How the plugin is published and
  installed is a separate packaging capability; defining delivery here would couple
  the content to a mechanism that should evolve independently.

There is one **accepted architectural limit**: enforcement depends on running
inside a plugin host that supports `PreToolUse` hooks, with the plugin installed.
Where that infrastructure is absent — a bare CLI, or a host without hook support —
proposal writes fall back to orientation's *guidance only*, with nothing in the
CLI broken. This is the dominant accepted residual risk: the guardrail strengthens
a *present* host and cannot retrofit absent infrastructure. And in a headless,
autonomous session with no human to answer, a gated write blocks pending
approval — that is the guardrail working as intended, not a defect.
